findings.name: exotic-source
findings.title: resolved from a git repository instead of the npm registry
findings.explanation: superset-frontend/package-lock.json resolves npm:dom-to-image@2.6.0 from a git repository (git+ssh://git@github.com/dmapper/dom-to-image.git#a7c386a8ea813930f05449ac71ab4be0c262dff3) rather than from the npm registry. None of the registry's protections apply to it: the release cannot be yanked, advisories are not matched against it, and there is no publisher, provenance or download history to compare with the previous version. The version number the lockfile records is what the fetched manifest claimed, not a version anyone published. The revision a7c386a8ea813930f05449ac71ab4be0c262dff3 is a full commit sha, so at least the content is pinned.

findings.name: exotic-source
findings.title: resolved from a URL instead of the npm registry
findings.explanation: superset-frontend/package-lock.json resolves npm:xlsx@0.20.3 from a URL (https://cdn.sheetjs.com/xlsx-0.20.3/xlsx-0.20.3.tgz) rather than from the npm registry. None of the registry's protections apply to it: the release cannot be yanked, advisories are not matched against it, and there is no publisher, provenance or download history to compare with the previous version. The version number the lockfile records is what the fetched manifest claimed, not a version anyone published. Whoever controls that URL can replace what it serves, and the lockfile would not change.

This is reported at info rather than at the level the policy sets for exotic-source, because that level is meant for a version fetched from a git repository or a URL, which is what a pull request can repoint under review, and not for an entry a monorepo or a bundling package manager writes for itself. An allow entry for exotic-source with a package glob takes it out of the report altogether.
